title: cultivar report.v1
description:
The envelope every cultivar report carries: what the report is about, when it was made, which regions were read, and what it assumed. A report body (a verdict, a price table, a benchmark) is attached by the command that produced it and is not part of this version.

Compatibility within report.v1 is additive: fields may be added, and enum-valued strings may gain members. Fields are never removed or renamed, no field's type changes, and no field's meaning changes. A consumer must ignore properties and enum members it does not recognize — new AWS states are the normal case, not an error. This is why no object here sets additionalProperties: false; a validator that rejects an added field would fail on exactly the change this policy permits.

The rule the whole format exists for: an absent value and zero are not interchangeable. Money that could not be resolved is null with provenance "unavailable", never 0.

schemaVersion.description: The wire format version. Independent of toolVersion: one schema outlives many builds.

kind.description: The report type, e.g. "compare" or "price". Lets one consumer handle a mixed directory of history records without inferring shape from content. Not an enum: new commands add kinds, and a reader that does not recognize one should skip the record rather than fail the directory.

toolVersion.description: The cultivar build that produced this report. A wrong number is traceable to a build only if the build is recorded.

generatedAt.description: When the report was produced, in UTC. This is the outer bound on freshness, not the freshness of the contents: each amount carries its own observedAt, and a price read from a cache is older than the report containing it. A consumer computes staleness from this and degrades its own claims accordingly.

account.description: The AWS account whose view this is. Optional, because prices are not account-specific — but quotas and offered-type sets are, so a quota finding is only interpretable with this recorded.

partition.description: The AWS partition, e.g. "aws", "aws-us-gov", "aws-cn". Optional. It matters because rates and available services differ by partition: a GovCloud run mislabelled as commercial produces a report full of prices that do not apply to it, and nothing in the report looks wrong. Read off the caller's ARN, never inferred from a region prefix. Constrained as a prefix rather than an enum because the aws-iso family has members this tool will never see, and an unrecognized partition is still a partition.

regions.description: The per-region outcome, in the order requested. Requested order rather than completion order: discovery fans out across goroutines, and a history log full of reordered-but-identical reports is one where a real change cannot be spotted in a diff.

timestamp.title: timestamp
timestamp.description:
An RFC 3339 instant in UTC, e.g. "2026-07-28T14:30:00Z".

UTC is required rather than merely preferred, which is why there is a pattern here and not only a format keyword: "format" is annotation-only by default in Draft 2020-12, so a validator running with defaults accepts any string at all — including "yesterday". A report whose timestamps mix frames sorts wrongly in the history log, and a naive comparison of two of them yields a negative age.

amount.title: amount
amount.description:
A number that knows where it came from. Every numeric quantity in a report is one of these; there is no bare float anywhere in the format.

value is nullable and always present. An unresolvable price serializes as null with provenance "unavailable", so a consumer that ignores provenance entirely still cannot mistake "no price exists" for "free" — p5e.48xlarge genuinely has no on-demand rate, and reporting that as 0 (or as a family-based guess) is the specific failure this format prevents.

The two states are enforced, not merely described: "unavailable" requires value to be null, and the other three require a number. A payload asserting a price with provenance "unavailable" is a contradiction, and the number is the part a careless consumer reads.

then.description: No value could be resolved, so there is no number to carry. Not 0, and not a family-based estimate.

else.description: A provenance that claims a value must carry one; a null here would decode as a zero price in any consumer that trusts the provenance.

value.description: The number, or null when provenance is "unavailable". Never a sentinel.

unit.description: The dimension. Not a label: amounts of differing units are never added, which is what catches adding a capacity block's upfront fee (USD) to an hourly rate (USD/hour).

provenance.description: Where the value came from. "live" was read from an API this run; "derived" was computed from other amounts, and is only as trustworthy as its worst input; "external" is a published third-party measurement, which can go stale without anything failing; "unavailable" means no value could be resolved.

source.description: The origin, or the reason there is no value. Free-form because its audience is a human checking a number against the console. For an unavailable amount this should say what would make the value obtainable — "no on-demand price exists; capacity-block only" rather than "lookup failed".

observedAt.description: When the value was read, or when an external figure was published. Absent for derived amounts, whose age is that of their inputs.

modelId.description: The Hugging Face repo id, e.g. "Qwen/Qwen3-32B".

bedrockModelId.description: The Bedrock foundation-model id when one exists. Absence is a finding rather than a gap: of 132 reverse-lookupable HF ids, 94 are marketplace-only, where you rent an instance and there is no token meter at all — so there is nothing for self-hosting to be compared against.

gated.description: Whether the repo requires a Hugging Face token. Blocks deploy, not comparison.

quantization.description: The checkpoint's quantization method, absent when unquantized.

observedAt.description: When the model metadata was read.

query.title: query
query.description:
The parameters that gated the result, as opposed to those that merely selected from it.

The distinction is load-bearing: asking for 8 instances where 1 was requested flipped "no capacity exists" to "offerings available", so a capacity report that does not state its instance count is not interpretable, and two runs with different counts look like AWS changed its mind.

regions.description: The region set as requested, in order. Kept alongside the per-region results so that a region which was asked for and vanished from the results is visible rather than reading as one with no capacity.

instanceCount.description: How many instances the query asked to be available at once. Absent when the dimension did not apply.

durationHours.description: The capacity-block duration requested. The *returned* duration belongs with each offering and never here: a 24h request came back with a 19h block, and dividing the fee by the requested duration understates the rate by 21%.

instanceTypes.description: An explicit type restriction, absent when the whole catalogue was enumerated. Recorded because "nothing fits" and "nothing fits among the three types you named" are different findings.

region.title: region
region.description: What happened when one region was queried.

state.description: The distinction that matters is between "asked, and there is nothing" (empty) and "never successfully asked" (failed). Both produce zero candidates, and conflating them turns an AccessDenied into a claim about AWS inventory — which then sends a user to a costlier region with no indication anything went wrong. More members arrive with the obtainability work; treat an unrecognized state as not-informative rather than failing.

considered.description: How many candidates were evaluated. Recorded even on failure, as zero, so a reader can see that a region contributing nothing contributed nothing because it was never read.

usable.description: How many candidates could serve the model. Never exceeds considered.

error.description: The failure text. Present exactly when state is "failed": a failure with no text cannot be told from an empty result, and a state that is not "failed" carrying an error is not ok.

assumptions.title: assumptions
assumptions.description:
The inputs that change the answer without changing any fact about AWS.

Structured rather than free-text because the history log has to be able to tell a price change from an assumption change. Two runs a day apart can disagree because a rate moved, because a region was added, or because the assumed traffic mix changed — and only the first two are facts about AWS.

inputTokenWeight.description: The input side of the traffic mix. Recorded as a weight pair rather than a rendered ratio so the arithmetic is reproducible without parsing a string, and so 6:2 and 3:1 do not read as different assumptions.

outputTokenWeight.description: The output side of the traffic mix. Bedrock meters input and output separately and output costs 4x input for Qwen3-32B, so any single $/1M figure has already assumed a shape: 3:1 blends to $0.2625/1M and 1:1 to $0.375, moving g7e.4xlarge's break-even from ~4,233 to ~2,963 tok/s. Note the direction — a pricier blend makes self-hosting *easier* to justify, so output-heavy traffic lowers the throughput bar.

utilization.description: The fraction of billed hours actually serving, in (0, 1]. There is no default anywhere in this tool: a silent 1.0 is the most flattering assumption available to a self-hosting recommendation and is almost never true.

contextTokens.description: Context length, which sizes the KV cache and so decides which instances qualify at all.

concurrency.description: Concurrent requests. At concurrency 8, Qwen3-32B's KV cache exceeds its own weights, so this changes the answer to "what fits" and not merely the throughput.

kvCacheDTypeBytes.description: KV cache element width in bytes (2 for fp16/bf16).

overheadFraction.description: Allowance for activations, CUDA graphs, and fragmentation. Recorded because it is an estimate, not a measurement.

throughput.description: The tok/s figure the comparison used, with its own provenance. Usually external (a published benchmark) or unavailable until one has been measured on this hardware — which is exactly why it must be visible rather than folded into the result.
